pattern: A step concludes a named thing is ABSENT after consulting one of the several views a distribution ships for that class of thing, and reports the conclusion as a fact about the distribution rather than as a fact about what it read. The disclosure is not what is missing -- such a step routinely names the files it opened and the zero it found in them -- so a reader auditing the artefact sees a complete, honest, wrong answer. What is missing is the comparison between the views that exist and the views that were opened.
docstring: A refusal that a declared name is ABSENT must be falsified against the views the step did not read -- and the falsification must ask through the DECLARATION GRAMMAR for that class of thing, never through a free-text search. It fires only when the refused name is actually DECLARED in a view the step did not open. The step already owns a parser for that grammar, so the check reuses it rather than inventing a search.
fix_action: On any verdict asserting a declared name is absent, take the name from the step's own artefact, enumerate the view directories of the resolved tree, subtract the ones the artefact says were read, and run the step's OWN declaration parser over the remainder. A declared hit means the refusal is false and names the file. No hit means the refusal stands and the check is silent.
measured_red_green: Both arms, with the negative control: PDK declares the name in the unread view -> FIRES, naming the file it is findable in. PDK declares it nowhere -> silent, and a genuine absence stays a genuine absence. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f1_final_probe.py`.
supersedes: An earlier version of this record proposed pinning the INPUT SET of a re-implementation against its upstream, caught by a set difference. That rule is REFUTED and the refutation is measured, not argued -- see `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f1_input_set_pin_REFUTED.txt`. Over its whole population of 5 modules it over-fires (43 findings under the natural scoping, 4 of 5 modules), and under every narrowing that reduces the over-firing it stops catching the defect it was written for: the control on the pre-fix tree reports an empty unaccounted list. The reason is structural -- the dropped variable is declared in the upstream PDK variable table and consumed in a shared helper, and is not a member of the upstream step's own declared inputs, so no set difference over that step's contract can contain it.
why_the_disclosure_form_is_not_the_rule: The finding was first generalised as 'a step that cannot find a declared thing must say WHICH views it read'. Driving the pre-fix producer, the refusal record already enumerated the exact file it read, the zero records found in it, and the empty result -- so a guard written to that rule runs clean on the buggy tree. The rule with teeth is not about naming what was read, it is about comparing it to what exists.
prior_art_checked: programs/gate_discloses_denominator_check.py, programs/_gate_denominator.py, programs/gate_zero_denominator_refuses_check.py, programs/_sweep_reach.py, programs/_shape_refusal.py -- five programs already own the DISCLOSURE half, and all five pass the pre-fix refusal, because the pre-fix refusal discloses. None of them compares what was read against what the distribution ships. No existing program makes that comparison.
formulation_history: THIRD formulation; the first two were swept and dropped, and one of them was adopted before it was swept, which is the mistake worth recording. (1) pin the input SET against upstream -- over-fires 4 of 5 and, once narrowed by upstream's own pdk flag, stops catching the defect at all. (2) a refusal must have READ every view -- fires on the defect, but sweeping it afterwards found 8 of the 10 in-scope programs read exactly one view for good reasons, so it is the same bug from the other side. Full sequence: `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f1_three_formulations.txt`.
false_positive_sweep: MEASURED on both real open PDKs in the pinned image, and it REFUTED the version I had published. The bare substring form over-fires: a short generic name hits an unrelated node-info file on both PDKs, and a plausible-but-absent name hits a circuit-simulator init file on one and a device-model file on the other. My claim that it was silent 'by construction' was an argument, not a measurement, and it was wrong. Asking the same question through the declaration grammar is clean on all four probes on both PDKs: the genuinely declared site fires with its size; the nonexistent name, the short generic name and the plausible-but-absent name are all silent. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f1_formulation3_fp_MEASURED.txt`.
measured_population: ONE, and this is the seventh correction to my own claims in this capture. The amended rule says the falsification must use the step's OWN declaration parser, so it applies only where such a parser exists. Of the 10 in-scope modules -- those that refuse on a named absence after a lookup into a distribution view -- exactly ONE owns a declaration parser. After four formulations, a red/green pair and a clean false-positive profile on two real distributions, F1 is a correct and well-measured SINGLE-SITE rule, not the general one I kept presenting it as.
the_widening_i_did_not_take: There is a stronger reading: rather than 'use the parser you have', demand that ANY step refusing on absence OWN a parser for the declaration grammar of the thing it refuses about. Under that reading the population is 10 and the rule fires on 9. I did NOT adopt it, and the reason is the whole history of this record: 9-of-10 is the exact shape that has been wrong six times in this capture, and I have not measured whether those 9 refuse about things that HAVE a declaration grammar at all -- several refuse about our own artefacts, which have none. The widening is named here so it is not lost, and flagged as UNSWEPT so nobody adopts it the way I adopted formulation 2.

pattern: A step re-implements an upstream computation and its arithmetic drifts from upstream's, in a direction no test covers because both agree on the inputs the tests use. The drift surfaces later as an unrelated refusal rather than as a wrong number, so it is attributed to the thing that refused instead of to the arithmetic. Here the along-the-row extent was taken from the ORIENTED footprint while upstream takes the master's width in both places it measures, on all four sides.
docstring: A re-implementation must DECLARE which upstream computation it mirrors and which primitive that computation measures with; the declaration is then checkable, and the check is a program. Detection without the declaration is NOT a program -- see the generality sweep -- so the deterministic work is the declaration format plus the checker that reads the named upstream file, confirms the named primitive is what it uses, and asserts our function does not transform it before aggregating.
fix_action: Walk the placement function's assignments and taint every name whose value flows from the orientation-dependent footprint helper. Refuse if the along-the-row extent is tainted. The upstream source that fixes the expected primitive is read from the pinned image at run time, not quoted from memory, and the gate returns NOT DETERMINED rather than PASS when it cannot read it.
measured_red_green: The one-computation pin, both arms: RED on origin/main (16 orientation-tainted names, the along-the-row extent among them), GREEN on the fix branch (2, both corner extents). `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f2_pin_probe.py`. That measurement stands; what it does NOT establish, and what my earlier version of this record wrongly claimed it did, is that the same predicate generalises.
upstream_confirmed_by_reading: The upstream side-arithmetic loop computes both a width and a height per instance and sums ONLY the width, in a loop that is side-agnostic. Read out of the pinned image on 2026-08-22, not cited from the source report.
prior_art_checked: VERIFIED over program bodies, not names: 6 programs both reference an upstream tree and use comparison language; reading all six, NONE pins one of our computations against upstream's. They cite upstream as documentation for what to expect -- the good habit -- and compare things within our own artefacts. `sta_engine_parity_check` pins two SHIPPED BINARIES against each other at run time; `_electrical_mention` and `_submission_template` stop two of OUR OWN halves drifting; `size_policy_drift_check` reconciles five of our own mechanisms; `ip_catalog_upstream_audit` pins vendored FILE COPIES by hash. No existing program makes an upstream computation's primitive executable against ours. Evidence: `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/prior_art_claims_VERIFIED.txt`.
why_a_cited_upstream_is_not_enough: MEASURED on the pre-fix tree: the correct upstream rule was written down ONE LINE ABOVE the code that violates it. The comment says the upstream primitive is used on every side; the next statement takes the orientation-dependent extent. The knowledge was present, correct, and cited -- it was simply not executable, and nothing compared the prose to the code. That is the whole case for this rule: the repo already has the discipline of reading upstream rather than remembering it, and several modules say so in those words, but the reading freezes into a comment at authoring time and is never re-checked against the code beneath it.
generality_sweep: MEASURED, and it refutes the generality my earlier version of this record claimed. The taint-walk predicate I measured red/green is written for ONE computation. Swept over the population -- the modules that cite an upstream computation by path -- the SHAPE it keys on (a value flowing through a transform into an aggregate) occurs at 224 sites. That shape is just what ordinary code looks like. A program cannot pick the one site of 224 that matters.
the_exact_decision_it_cannot_make: Named as the ladder requires, rather than waved at. INPUT the program would see: the AST of our module and the text of the upstream file. DECISION it cannot make from that input: the CORRESPONDENCE -- which of our functions re-implements which upstream loop. Neither text declares it. Our function does not say which upstream loop it mirrors, and the upstream loop does not say what re-implements it. BUT THAT MISSING INPUT IS DECLARABLE, not unknowable, which is why this stays Bucket A rather than becoming a judgement call: the information already exists in the module as PROSE -- it cites the upstream file by path, and on the pre-fix tree the comment one line above the defect names the correct primitive. Turning that prose into a declaration is a one-line change per site and converts an undecidable detection into a decidable check.

title: WITHDRAWN: a forked-tool defect that was the tool behaving as documented
why_discard: I filed this as a Bucket-T defect against a forked tool: its two named rotation arguments appeared to be applied to each other's rows. Every measurement behind it is correct -- seven processes, row identity confirmed by die position, reproduced on two builds. The INFERENCE from them was not. The tool's own documented contract, fetched at the pinned commit, defines the argument named 'horizontal' as applying to the horizontally-ORIENTED PADS, which sit on the EAST and WEST rows -- not to the horizontal rows. Under that convention every number I measured is the documented behaviour, including the exact default orientation I found on the western pad, which the documentation predicts because the caller passes the same site to both arguments. The source is not crossed either. I dumped the tool's script layer, confirmed it passes the arguments in declared order, and then reasoned about what the argument NAMES must mean without ever fetching the page that defines them. Calling an inference 'measured' because the numbers under it were measured is the failure. This is NOT discarded as 'not a plugin gap' or 'design-side' -- it is discarded as REFUTED, and the real defect it was masking is a separate record in this batch. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3_bucket_T_WITHDRAWN.txt`.

pattern: A step accepts a config variable the tool underneath does not honour as named, and proceeds without saying so. The author who set it is told nothing, and the artefact records a value that did not reach the geometry. The mirrored failure is a step that discloses the defect for the ONE variable it happened to measure and leaves the sibling variable, which is the one the tool actually mis-applies, unguarded.
docstring: The degradation contract for a config variable a step accepts but cannot honour. At the value indistinguishable from never having set it: PROCEED, and carry the non-honouring record, with its measurement, in EVERY report the step emits INCLUDING its skips, because a disclosure present only on the happy path is not a disclosure. At any deliberately declared other value: exit 2 NOT DETERMINED naming the variable, never 0 and never 1, because being unable to honour a request is neither a pass nor a finding about the design. The rule is the contract, not the one variable: every variable the same tool call carries is in scope, not only the one that was measured.
fix_action: Require, for any step that declares a variable unhonoured: the non-honouring record is a key of the BASE report template rather than of one branch, so it survives every early return; a deliberately declared value exits 2; and the guarded set covers every variable passed in the same tool call as the measured one. Drive the step's skip path and its proceed path and require the key in both, and drive it with a declared value and require exit 2.
why_this_rule_and_not_the_one_variable: The ruling that produced this was written for one variable. MEASURED here, the sibling variable is the one that silently changes the geometry the ruling was protecting, and the shipped guard does not cover it, so a run that declares the sibling and leaves the measured one alone passes the guard and gets an artefact whose recorded orientation contradicts the tool. Generalising the rule to the tool CALL rather than the variable closes that.
prior_art_checked: `adder_map_techmap.py` states the general rule in prose in its own header and enforces it for its ONE knob, by requiring evidence from the tool's own log. Three other modules state a version of it for their own case. No module inherits it, and no program checks it. `waiver_staleness.py` refuses a waiver whose reason no longer holds, and `dead_timing_constant_warn.py` finds declared constants nothing references; neither asks whether a declared input REACHED the tool.
measured_population: ONE. Read at the level of the rule's own definition -- a step that OWNS a config variable the tool does not honour -- exactly one of the four modules the sweep found is an instance, and it already implements half the contract by hand: it verifies against the tool's own log and emits `applied: false` with the reason. The other three MENTION the phenomenon in prose, as the justification for a remedy or as a reason not to pick one; they own no such knob and are consumers of the lesson, not instances of the class.
failure_signature: Measured across the three genuine instances, they share one shape: the artefact is INDISTINGUISHABLE from never having set the input. One produced a byte-identical netlist and cost 22 percent of a timing path before anyone looked. There is nothing in the output to review, which is why three separate people had to rediscover it.
landing_status: Correct but RED on the current tree, and the red is 3 true positives across 4 modules rather than a false one: none meets either half of the contract. This supersedes an earlier claim in this batch that the rule had no population, which was made without measuring and was wrong, and a later one that the population was four, which counted a case that is not a member.
its_motivating_case_is_not_a_member: STATED BECAUSE IT CHANGES WHAT THIS RULE IS. The case that produced this rule -- the pad rotation -- turned out NOT to be an instance of the class. The tool honours that variable exactly as it documents; what was wrong was our own mapping of it to the wrong pair of sides. So the class was discovered from a FALSE premise and then validated by a sweep that found three genuine members that have nothing to do with pads. The rule stands on those three, not on the case that suggested it, and anyone weighing it should weigh it on them. Earlier versions of this record counted the pad ring as a fourth instance; it is not one.
how_the_0_of_4_was_established: SOURCE-level, and labelled as such. I tried to confirm it at runtime after writing that a finding is not a finding until it has been run, and the run came back VACUOUS -- the program examined no blocks, so its silence about the construct is the absence of a run, not evidence of silence on a real one. Counting it would have retired the question with the authority of having checked. Confirming this at runtime needs a real per-instance project fixture, which this capture does not build. Named and left open. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3b_run_was_vacuous_NOT_EVIDENCE.txt`.
supersedes_my_own_zero_of_four: An earlier version of this record said 0 of 4 carry the non-honouring as a machine-readable record, and that 'discovered four times and absorbed zero times' was the argument for the rule. Both are wrong on half (a). The grep behind them enumerated NEGATIVE spellings of the concept -- inert, not_applied, unhonoured -- and the instance spells it POSITIVELY as `applied: false`. No list of spellings closes that hole; running the program does, immediately. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3b_zero_of_four_REFUTED.txt`.
the_honest_argument_now: Weaker than what I published, and still real: one module implemented half the contract by hand, three did not, none INHERITS it, and nothing in the repo makes them agree. That is what a shared contract is for. The rule should be argued on that, not on a zero that was never true.
what_this_costs_the_rule: I called this the item most worth someone's time, and a class discovered repeatedly and absorbed zero times. Neither holds. A rule with one instance, where that instance already does half of it, is not a gap -- it is a description of something that works. Its motivating case was separately withdrawn as not a member. The record is kept, at its true size, rather than deleted: the half it does NOT do (the exit-code tier, which that instance gets wrong in both directions -- rc 1 when unhonoured, rc 0 when it cannot tell) is still real and still unowned. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3b_population_is_ONE_not_four.txt`.
the_different_and_weaker_claim_that_surv: All four modules do share something, and it is not this rule: each encodes a fact about a tool not honouring something as PROSE, in whichever module discovered it, and nothing shares those facts between them. That is a real pattern about where tool-behaviour knowledge lives. It has no exit-code tier and no report key and it must not be argued as if it were the degradation contract -- which is exactly what my earlier count did, by counting consumers as instances.

design: (found while capturing, not one of the three findings)
pattern: A validator advertises an accepted vocabulary of the form PREFIX:IDENTIFIER, one prefix per namespace, and its character class cannot express the identifiers of one of those namespaces. The advertised form is then unusable for every member of that namespace, and the failure is invisible from the validator's side: it reports a well-formed refusal naming the very form the author used, so the author reads it as their own mistake and substitutes a different prefix. Nobody files it, because each individual author works around it in one line.
docstring: Every prefix a component-vocabulary validator advertises must accept the identifiers of the namespace that prefix names. Deterministic form: for each advertised prefix, enumerate the namespace it points at from that namespace's own source of truth, and require the validator to accept every member. A prefix whose namespace is empty or unenumerable is refused as unverifiable rather than assumed fine.
fix_action: Enumerate each namespace from its declared source and assert the validator accepts every member, as a test that fails when either the regex or the namespace changes. Do NOT simply widen the character class in isolation: the test is what keeps the two in step, and the widening without it would drift again the next time a namespace gains a character.
measured: The advertised form for the step namespace admits 0 of the 39 step ids in the capture routing table, and 6 of the 69 ids in the canonical flow are inexpressible -- every one of the six a dotted inserted step, one of which is the step this whole capture is about. No shipped record in the backlog corpus uses that prefix, which is what an unusable form looks like from the outside: not an error, an absence.
why_not_fixed_here: The fix would widen a regex, and it would do so on the exact night that regex refused a record of mine. The standing rule is that a red is never made to go away by relaxing what asks the question, and it binds hardest when the red is my own. Captured, measured, and left red.
prior_art_checked: No program compares an accepted-vocabulary regex against the namespace it names. `programs/p0_gate_invocability_drift_check.py` is the nearest neighbour -- it pins the gates a registry declares but cannot invoke -- and it is about argv, not about an identifier grammar.
measured_population: ONE. Swept for validators carrying a PREFIX:IDENTIFIER alternation: exactly one in 1232 programs. This is a real defect with a real measurement, but it is a SINGLE INSTANCE, not a class with a corpus, and it is recorded as such rather than dressed as a general rule. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f4_population_MEASURED.txt`.

pattern: A step re-implements a tool's interface and inverts one of its CONVENTIONS -- which of two symmetric cases a named input applies to. Both names exist on both sides and both sides accept both values, so nothing type-checks and nothing errors. It is invisible wherever the two inputs carry the same value, which is the default, so the defect ships and waits for the first author who sets exactly one of them. Every downstream artefact is then internally consistent and disagrees with the tool.
docstring: A re-implementation must not invert its upstream's convention. Where an upstream input selects between two symmetric cases, the case our step applies it to must be the case the upstream documents it for. The comparison is between two enumerable mappings and it is a program's decision once the upstream mapping is declared -- which is the same declare-then-check shape the arithmetic pin in this batch arrives at.
fix_action: Declare the upstream mapping beside our own and assert they agree, and take the upstream half from the tool's DOCUMENTED contract rather than from the argument names. Here, measured side by side: ours sends the horizontal-named variable to the south and north sides and the vertical-named one to the west and east sides; the tool documents the opposite for both. The two mappings are four entries each, so the check is a dict comparison.
measured: Ours, unchanged on both the current tree and the fix branch, maps the horizontal-named rotation to SOUTH/NORTH and the vertical-named one to WEST/EAST. The tool documents the horizontal-named argument as applying to EAST and WEST and the vertical-named one to NORTH and SOUTH, and its source assigns the rows that way. Inverted on both axes. Invisible at the default because both variables are R0 there. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3_bucket_T_WITHDRAWN.txt`, `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/openroad_pad_README_at_pinned_commit.md`.
consequence_for_the_shipped_fix: MEASURED by running the pin against both trees, not argued. On the current tree the mapping is inverted on both axes. On the un-landed fix branch it is STILL RED, and differently: the horizontal-named variable still drives the wrong two sides, and the vertical-named one now drives NOTHING -- the fix pinned those sides to a measured constant, which removes the variable's effect rather than routing it correctly, because it had concluded the variable was inert. It is not inert; it is misrouted by us, and in the tool it drives the sides the fix left to the other variable. A run that declares it is then refused rc 2 -- a refusal of a declaration the tool would have honoured. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3c_the_fix_branch_does_not_resolve_it.txt`.
prior_art_checked: No program compares our mapping of an upstream input against the upstream's documented one. This is the third instance in this capture of one class -- a re-implementation drifting from its upstream -- after the input set and the arithmetic, and it is the one that drifted on the CONVENTION.
checked_at_the_layer_we_reimplement: The first version of this record compared our mapping against the TOOL's documentation. But we re-implement the FLOW layer above the tool, and that is the layer that names the variable -- so if IT documented the term our way, the attribution would move off us. Read: the flow layer says 'Rotation to apply to the horizontal sites', the same phrase the tool uses, adds no redefinition, and passes the value straight through. It is consistent with the tool. Ours is inverted, and the attribution stands. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3c_checked_at_the_layer_we_reimplement.txt`.
how_the_inversion_happened_and_the_gener: The layer we read documents the term TERSELY -- 'the horizontal sites' -- and never says which sides those are. The disambiguation exists but lives ONE LAYER DOWN, in the tool's command reference, which expands it as the pads on the east and west rows. A reader working from the layer they re-implement has a description that is complete-looking, authoritative and insufficient, and the natural reading of 'horizontal' is the horizontal ROWS. Generalised, and it has nothing to do with pads: WHEN THE LAYER YOU RE-IMPLEMENT DOCUMENTS A TERM TERSELY, THE DEFINITION MAY LIVE IN THE LAYER BELOW IT -- a description that does not enumerate its cases is not a definition, however authoritative its source. This is the same substitution I made myself one level up when I filed a defect against the tool after reading its argument NAMES rather than its argument DEFINITIONS: twice in one capture, at two layers, taking a name for a specification.
pinning_test: `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/candidate_tests/superseded_f3c_side_to_variable_mapping.py` -- RED on both trees, kept out of `programs/tests/` because a red test there blocks every push. It reads OUR mapping out of the source rather than restating it, so it does not drift into agreeing with a copy of itself.

pattern: A re-implementation derives the opposite of a symmetric pair with the wrong TRANSFORM -- a half turn where the upstream mirrors, or the reverse. For a rectangular footprint the two occupy the SAME bounding box, so every geometric check downstream agrees under both and the defect passes fit, spacing, abutment and coverage alike. What differs is where the cell's PINS end up. The artefact is internally consistent, passes its own gates, and faces the wrong way.
docstring: Where a step derives one member of a symmetric pair from the other, the transform must be the transform the upstream uses. Mirroring and half-turning are interchangeable for a bounding box and are not interchangeable for a cell. The check compares two named transforms and is a program's decision once the upstream one is declared -- the same declare-then-check shape the other pins in this batch arrive at.
fix_action: Declare the upstream transform beside ours and assert they agree. Upstream derives the opposite side by MIRRORING on both axes -- north from south by a flip about X, east from west by a flip about Y -- and states it in two lines of its own source. Ours applies a half turn on both axes through a helper whose docstring says 'one quarter turn clockwise'. Any bounding-box-based test will pass under either, so the test that pins this must compare the ORIENTATION TOKEN, never the extents. And the pinning test must compare the ORIENTATION TOKEN, never the extents: an extent-based assertion passes under both and reads as coverage.
measured: At the default, with no pad rotation declared at all: ours records the south side as R0 and the north side as R180; the tool, in its own process, places the south pad at R0 and the north pad at MX. A half turn is not a mirror. The tool's source states the rule directly for both axes. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3d_mirror_vs_halfturn_MEASURED.txt`, `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3c_our_recorded_orientation_probe.py`.
severity_relative_to_this_batch: Every other finding in this capture needs somebody to DECLARE something before it becomes visible. This one is present at the DEFAULT, with no pad configuration written, on both axes -- and it survives every geometric gate the step owns because a half turn and a mirror share a bounding box.
prior_art_checked: No program compares a derived transform against its upstream's. This is the fourth instance in this capture of one class -- a re-implementation drifting from the upstream whose behaviour it claims to reproduce -- after the input set, the arithmetic, and the convention.
why_the_gate_cannot_catch_it: READ OUT OF THE GATE rather than asserted. The producer's gate is the only thing in this step that looks at orientation, and what it does is convert it to an EXTENT and compare extents. The helper it uses swaps axes for exactly one set of orientations, and both the half turn and the mirror are outside that set, so both yield the same unswapped extent. The gate is not merely silent -- it is structurally incapable of seeing the difference, because it reduces the orientation to the one quantity in which the two are identical. Every other check in the step is bounding-box arithmetic and is blind for the same reason. `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-padring/evidence/f3d_the_gate_is_structurally_blind.txt`.
scope_stated: SINGLE SITE, said plainly so this is not read as more general than it was measured. It is the opposite-side derivation in one function. I have NOT swept the repo for other places that derive one member of a symmetric pair from the other, and the comparable sweep earlier in this capture found that shape at 224 sites -- which is what ordinary code looks like. So its value is in the DEFECT it names, not in a class it heads.
